cosy-lesson.title: Do We Carry a Collective Self-Guilt for the Planet?

cosy-teacher-notes.p: Stage aim: to introduce the topic and clarify key target vocabulary for the session.

cosy-slide.cosy-instruction: Review the key vocabulary for this session below:

cosy-blockquote.p: Complicity – the fact or condition of being involved with others in an activity that is unlawful or morally wrong.

p.em: Example: Our daily consumer decisions carry a quiet complicity in global manufacturing waste.

cosy-blockquote.p: Anxiety – a feeling of worry, nervousness, or unease, typically about an upcoming event or something with an uncertain outcome.

p.em: Example: Reading about the melting glaciers filled her with a persistent sense of eco-related anxiety.

cosy-blockquote.p: Hypocrisy – the practice of claiming to have moral standards or beliefs to which one's own behavior does not conform.

p.em: Example: Flying on private jets while preaching climate awareness is the ultimate form of modern hypocrisy.

cosy-blockquote.p: Inevitably – as is certain to happen; unavoidably.

p.em: Example: When millions of individuals use disposable cups, it inevitably leads to massive environmental damage.

cosy-blockquote.p: Impunity – exemption from punishment or freedom from the injurious consequences of an action.

p.em: Example: Huge global conglomerates pollute local water supplies with apparent impunity.

cosy-blockquote.p: Apathy – lack of interest, enthusiasm, or concern.

p.em: Example: Faced with constant devastating headlines, it is easy to retreat into a protective state of apathy.

cosy-blockquote.p: Accomplice – a person who helps another commit a crime or do something morally wrong.

p.em: Example: By ignoring eco-friendly regulations, we become an accomplice to the destruction of local habitats.

cosy-blockquote.p: Culpable – deserving blame; guilty of a misdeed.

p.em: Example: Are we morally culpable for historical carbon emissions that we had no hand in starting?

cosy-blockquote.p: Erase – to completely remove or destroy something.

p.em: Example: No amount of recycling can completely erase the carbon footprint of an international flight.

cosy-blockquote.p: Privilege – a special right, advantage, or exceptional immunity granted or available only to a particular group.

p.em: Example: Having the mental space to worry about eco-anxiety is itself a form of geographic privilege.

cosy-teacher-notes.p: Stage aim: pair/group discussion on core session themes.

cosy-slide.cosy-group-instruction: In pairs or small breakout groups, discuss the following questions:

ol.li:
Is our constant consumer anxiety a productive force for global change, or is it just a psychological burden that paralyzes us?
★ Have you ever felt a deep sense of personal guilt while buying something wrapped in excessive plastic?

How do we navigate our daily complicity in global systems that pollute the earth and support economic exploitation?
★ Do you think about the ethical background of the companies you buy clothing or electronics from?

Is it possible to live in modern society without falling into some degree of moral hypocrisy?
★ Have you ever felt like a hypocrite for advocating for the environment while living a high-consumption lifestyle?

Does our access to unprecedented digital information inevitably make us feel responsible for tragedies occurring thousands of miles away?
★ How do you protect your mental peace when the global news cycle becomes overwhelmingly negative?

Why do global corporations operate with apparent impunity, while individual citizens bear the psychological weight of saving the planet?
★ Do you believe that individual actions, like recycling, actually make a difference compared to corporate regulations?

Is the modern rise of social media apathy a natural self-defense mechanism against constant exposure to global suffering?
★ Have you ever felt the urge to delete all news apps and social media accounts just to escape global problems?

When we buy fast-fashion or cheap imported goods, do we become an active accomplice in labor exploitation?
★ Have you ever tried to source your clothes from local, ethical, or second-hand shops?

At what point does a passive citizen become morally culpable for the aggressive policies of their government or the actions of global alliances?
★ How do you handle conversations about political and social conflicts with people who hold opposing views?

Can a simple lifestyle change ever truly erase the carbon footprint of an average modern human being?
★ What is one daily habit you have changed specifically to reduce your impact on the environment?

How should we utilize our global privilege to assist less fortunate communities without falling into the trap of superficial savior complexes?
★ In what ways do you feel your geographic and economic background has shaped your view of global crises?

cosy-teacher-notes.p: Stage aim: deeper debate and statement evaluation in pairs/groups.

cosy-slide.cosy-group-instruction: In pairs, debate and state whether you agree or disagree with these statements:

ol.li:
Traditional communities focused their moral concerns entirely on local, immediate neighbors, whereas modern global citizens carry the psychological burden of the entire world.
★ Do you think our brains were designed to process global suffering, or are we experiencing information overload?

Older generations worked with tangible resources and witnessed the direct consequences of their labor, while modern digital workers are isolated from the physical impact of their choices.
★ Do you prefer physical, hands-on activities, or does your daily life mostly take place behind a screen?

Traditional societies relied on a simple worldview of local survival, whereas modern life is plagued by chronic moral anxiety about global climate catastrophes.
★ Are you optimistic or pessimistic about the future of our planet over the next fifty years?

While past generations lived with limited geographic awareness, modern technology inevitably connects our everyday consumer choices to distant environmental degradation.
★ How often do you think about the physical origin of the food on your dinner plate?

In traditional settings, waste was practically non-existent due to scarcity, whereas modern consumerism has created a waste crisis that makes every citizen feel like an active accomplice.
★ Have you ever participated in a zero-waste challenge or tried to live completely plastic-free?

Past eras defined moral duty through religious or tribal codes, while modern secular individuals must construct their own ethical boundaries amidst a sea of global information.
★ Do you find it difficult to decide what is "right" and "wrong" when considering complex global economics?

Older societies experienced localized hardships with a sense of collective resilience, whereas modern individuals often suffer from a lonely, internalized guilt regarding global crises.
★ Do you have a supportive community or friends with whom you can openly discuss your fears about the world?

While ancient leaders ruled with localized power, modern global elites operate with systemic impunity, leaving ordinary citizens feeling both powerless and morally culpable.
★ What is one global issue where you feel completely powerless to make a difference?

Traditional life prioritized ancestral continuity, but modern privilege demands instant gratification at the expense of future generations' survival.
★ In what ways do you think we are currently robbing future generations of a healthy planet?

In the past, communities had a high tolerance for natural weather cycles, whereas modern scientific awareness has eliminated moral apathy, making us feel that every storm is our fault.
★ Do you believe humanity can successfully unite to solve climate change, or are we too divided?
